Typically, neonatal jaundice presents on the second or third day of life.

qs.q: What is the primary substance that accumulates and causes the yellow coloration of the skin and sclera in neonatal jaundice?
qs.e: Neonatal jaundice results from the accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin, which is neurotoxic. Conjugated bilirubin is typically associated with cholestatic processes.

qs.q: An infant is born to a mother living at a high altitude and has an older sibling who required treatment for neonatal jaundice. How do these factors affect the infant?
o: They lower the clinical risk of developing clinically significant jaundice.
They increase the incidence and familial risk of neonatal jaundice.
They alter the diagnostic efficacy of transcutaneous bilirubinometry.
They specifically cause conjugated hyperbilirubinemia rather than unconjugated.
qs.e: Geographic location at high altitude and a family history of a sibling requiring treatment for jaundice both increase the incidence of neonatal jaundice. These factors raise the clinical index of suspicion.

qs.q: In what anatomical sequence does neonatal jaundice typically progress across the body during physical examination?
o: Trunk first, followed by the extremities and finally the face
Face and forehead first, then gradually to the trunk and extremities
Lower extremities first, moving upward toward the head
Simultaneously across all dermatomes regardless of bilirubin level
qs.e: Neonatal jaundice first becomes visible in the face and forehead and then gradually becomes visible on the trunk and extremities. It disappears in the opposite direction.

qs.q: What is the primary role of a direct antiglobulin test (DAT) in the workup of an infant with neonatal jaundice?
o: Screening for galactosemia and metabolic blockages
Detecting immune-mediated hemolytic disease via Coombs test
qs.e: The direct antiglobulin test (DAT), also known as the direct Coombs test, helps evaluate for immune-mediated hemolysis in the infant. It is part of the additional laboratory studies.

qs.q: An infant with neonatal jaundice is found to have elevated aspartate aminotransferase (ASAT) and alanine aminotransferase (ALAT) levels. What underlying process does this suggest?
qs.e: ASAT and ALAT levels are elevated in hepatocellular disease, whereas alkaline phosphatase and GGT are often elevated in cholestatic disease.

qs.q: Which form of bilirubin is primarily responsible for the yellow coloration and neurotoxicity associated with severe neonatal jaundice?
qs.e: Unconjugated bilirubin accumulates and is neurotoxic, potentially causing kernicterus. Conjugated forms are water-soluble and do not share this specific neurotoxic profile.

qs.q: When assessing the progression of neonatal jaundice through physical examination, where does visible jaundice typically first become apparent?
qs.e: Neonatal jaundice first becomes visible in the face and forehead and gradually extends to the trunk and extremities. Blanching via skin pressure aids in identifying this underlying color.

qs.q: Which population group has a recognized higher incidence of neonatal jaundice compared to others?
qs.e: The incidence of neonatal jaundice is higher in East Asians and American Indians and lower in Africans and African Americans. Geography and genetics also play key roles in varied incidences.

ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Neonatal jaundice is excess bilirubin in a newborn, usually benign but can progress to kernicterus if untreated. Clinicians must assess severity, identify cause, and initiate timely phototherapy or exchange transfusion.

sections.p: Jaundice is visible yellowing of skin and sclera due to unconjugated bilirubin. Diagnosis is clinical plus serum total bilirubin (TB) and direct fraction. A TB >15 mg/dL in a term infant warrants treatment.
b: Serum TB >15 mg/dL in term newborn

t.b: Measures bilirubin load; high levels predict risk of neurotoxicity
Differentiates hepatic vs hemolytic causes; >1.0 mg/dL suggests hepatic dysfunction

sections.p: The Bhutani nomogram stratifies risk by age in hours and TB. Low risk (<10 mg/dL at 24 h), moderate (10–15 mg/dL), high (>15 mg/dL).

t.b: Predicts need for phototherapy; high values trigger treatment

sections.p: In term infants, physiologic immaturity of UDP‑glucuronosyltransferase is common. Pathologic causes include hemolysis, infection, G6PD deficiency, ABO incompatibility, sepsis, and biliary atresia.

t.b: Detects spherocytes or schistocytes indicating hemolysis

sections.p: Early‑onset (within 24 h) jaundice suggests hemolysis or infection. Late‑onset (after 48 h) points to biliary atresia or sepsis. Phototherapy is started when TB exceeds risk thresholds.
Baseline labs guide etiology and monitor therapy. In low‑resource settings, point‑of‑care bilirubin and hemoglobin are essential.

t.b: Assesses anemia and reticulocytosis; high retics suggest hemolysis
Positive indicates immune hemolysis; negative suggests non‑immune causes
Elevated ALT/AST point to hepatic injury

sections.p: Kernicterus, acute bilirubin encephalopathy, and death are the most feared complications. Prompt treatment prevents them.

t.b: Detects early signs of bilirubin encephalopathy

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. Phototherapy is first‑line for moderate cases; exchange transfusion is reserved for severe or refractory jaundice. Supportive care includes hydration and monitoring.

t.b: Higher intensity lowers bilirubin faster; monitor skin temperature to avoid overheating

sections.p: Re‑check TB 48–72 h after treatment. Counsel parents on breastfeeding, early feeding, and avoiding delayed cord clamping. Screen for hemolytic disease in subsequent pregnancies.
Physiologic jaundice, neonatal sepsis, and congenital hypothyroidism can mimic or coexist with jaundice.
Low bilirubin in a sick infant may be due to hemolysis masking high total bilirubin. Point‑of‑care devices can underestimate TB in dark‑skinned babies.
b: Dark skin pigmentation may reduce accuracy of visual assessment

whenToSeekHelp: Severe jaundice (TB >20 mg/dL), rapid rise in bilirubin, lethargy, poor feeding, seizures, or any sign of neurologic dysfunction

faq.a: When TB exceeds the age‑specific risk threshold on the Bhutani nomogram or is >15 mg/dL in a term infant.
Breastfeeding itself does not worsen jaundice; inadequate intake can delay clearance, so frequent feeds are encouraged.
